title: Feedback That Changes Behaviour

audience.who: corporate employees who give feedback to peers or direct reports
audience.knows: feedback matters but often delivers it as general praise or criticism
audience.cares_about: getting a colleague to actually do something differently without damaging the relationship

outcome: After watching, a viewer can take a vague comment they were about to give and rewrite it as feedback naming a specific observed behaviour, its effect, and one concrete next step.
through_line: Feedback that only moves feelings leaves behaviour untouched; naming what someone did, what it caused and what to try next is what gives them something to change.

arc_plan.what: A manager gives a colleague a warm, vague comment after a meeting, and the colleague nods, feels fine, and repeats the same habit next week.
Tell the viewer they will leave able to turn that kind of comment into feedback the colleague can act on, using the same colleague and meeting.
Link the viewer's own memory of receiving vague feedback to why good intentions did not change anything in the opening scene.
Rework the same meeting comment in steps: name the observed behaviour, state its effect on others, then agree one concrete next step, each step visibly changing the one comment.
Show a new vague comment about a different small workplace moment and let the viewer choose which rewrite names behaviour, effect and next step.
Prompt the viewer to pick one real piece of feedback they owe this week and rewrite it the same way before saying it.
Return to the opening colleague and meeting, now with the reworked feedback, and show the habit changing the following week.

must_cover.what: Why vague or purely feelings-based feedback fails to change what someone does
Feedback anchored in specific observed behaviour rather than character or personality
Stating the effect the behaviour had on others or the work
Ending with a concrete next step the person can try
A checkable example where the viewer picks the stronger rewrite

must_avoid: Statistics or research figures without a source
Made-up sayings presented as real research
Opening with a textbook meaning of the word feedback or an agenda
Talking down to the viewer like a trainer with a checklist
Naming a specific feedback model as if it were the only valid one
example_posture: One running example: a colleague, one recurring meeting habit, and one comment reworked step by step. Realistic and low-drama; the check uses a different small workplace moment.
visual_direction: Story-cartoon look: a person in a recognisable workplace situation, one comment that visibly changes as each part is added, a before and after of the same scene, and a simple view of next week showing the habit shifting. One loud thing at a time.
voice_note: Mentor: a warm, experienced colleague who has got this wrong too, direct and unhurried, never a lecturer.
open_questions: No look preference was given for story intensity or faces versus none; classic approach assumed, newer treatments to be offered later.
Whether the organisation uses a particular feedback model is unknown.

inferred: running example of a meeting habit
the three-part structure of behaviour, effect, next step as the build
